lessons.title: Review — six verbs, one ending
lessons.gloss: review — the -go club is complete, and it was never a club to begin with

segments.text: Nothing new in this chapter. Say the yo forms of the three verbs you have just met: poner, salir, venir.
The set is closed. Six of the commonest verbs in Spanish put an unexpected -go on the yo form and nowhere else:

utterances: verb: tener. yo: tengo. and the rest behaves: normally.
verb: hacer. yo: hago. and the rest behaves: normally.
verb: decir. yo: digo. and the rest behaves: normally.
verb: poner. yo: pongo. and the rest behaves: normally.
verb: salir. yo: salgo. and the rest behaves: normally.
verb: venir. yo: vengo. and the rest behaves: normally.

segments.text: Six verbs, one oddity, and it lives in exactly one slot. That is a much smaller thing to carry than "six irregular verbs."
Here is what the six chapters could not show you separately.

They are not a family. Nobody decided these six belonged together. They came from different Latin verbs, by different routes, and arrived at the same ending by accident — a g that was already in some of the stems, and a sound change that pulled the others into line behind them.

The club is a result, not a rule. Spanish learners are taught "the -go verbs" as though someone had drawn up a membership list; what actually happened is that six unrelated words drifted into the same shape and then reinforced each other.
That is worth knowing for a practical reason: it tells you the list is closed. A pattern with a cause keeps recruiting. A pattern that is an accident stops.

segments.text: Until the six run together as one list.

segments.prompt: How many verbs are in the -go set?

feedback.correct: Six — and the set is closed.
feedback.incorrect: Six: tener, hacer, decir, poner, salir, venir.

segments.prompt: Which slot does the -go appear in?

feedback.correct: Only the yo slot. Everything else is regular.

segments.prompt: Are these six related to each other?

feedback.correct: Right — which is why the list is closed rather than growing.
feedback.incorrect: No. They came from different Latin verbs and drifted into the same shape.

segments.text: How many verbs take -go? (Six.) In how many slots? (One — the yo form.) And why does the list not grow? (Because it was never a rule — six unrelated verbs happened to converge.)

lessons.title: Practice — putting, leaving, and coming in the singular
lessons.gloss: singular putting, leaving, and coming, plus the six learned yo forms

segments.text: This checkpoint adds nothing. Retrieve the three bounded singular sets first. Only then widen the memory comparison from three learned yo forms to six.

blocks.title: Grammar Lens: the complete frame for this chapter

segments.text: putting or placing: pongo, pones, pone.
leaving or going out: salgo, sales, sale.
coming: vengo, vienes, viene.
known-word contrast: Salgo de Madrid. Vengo de Madrid.
known singular comparison: vengo / tengo, vienes / tienes, viene / tiene.

Now that all three new verbs have been taught, the learned yo comparison can grow to exactly tengo, hago, digo, pongo, salgo, vengo. It remains a retrieval aid, not a rule for predicting any unseen verb.
Plural persons, full boot diagrams, reflexive clothing expressions, house and table nouns, clock times, dinner vocabulary, and other unseen contexts remain outside this checkpoint.

blocks.title: The words, taken apart — retrieve the history

segments.text: poner continues Latin pōnere, the placing family of position.
salir continues Latin salīre, the leaping family of salient.
venir continues Latin venīre, the coming family of convene.
different inherited histories and analogy let the six known yo forms converge on -go; the shared shape does not make a productive prediction rule.

segments.text: Give all three new singular sets. (Pongo, pones, pone; salgo, sales, sale; vengo, vienes, viene.) Which six learned yo forms now share -go? (Tengo, hago, digo, pongo, salgo, vengo.) Why is the list a memory aid rather than a prediction rule? (Different histories converged on one shape.) The next chapter may now introduce a new time frame without borrowing any plural form from this chapter.
